Asthma & Bronchiectasis

A lecture-anchored, mechanism-first guide built to move from recognition to prediction: why the airway narrows, why it stays dilated, what the tests are really measuring, and which clue actually separates the look-alikes.

Professor materials firstLight / print-friendlyDelayed answer + source reveal33 practice questionsOffline / self-contained
1 • Start here

Build the airway story before memorizing labels

The lecture is easiest if you keep one distinction in your head: bronchiectasis is permanent structural destruction; asthma is variable hyperresponsive obstruction that may remodel over time.

Bronchiectasis map
clearance failure / obstruction → infection → inflammation → wall destruction → permanent dilation → worse clearance
Asthma map
trigger → hyperresponsive airway → bronchoconstriction + mucus + edema → variable obstruction → repeated inflammation → remodeling
Question-solving map
pattern → reversible vs permanent → inflammation / clearance mechanism → decisive test or image → treatment logic

Fast stem approach

1. Decide the time pattern.
Episodic / nocturnal / trigger-dependent strongly supports asthma. Daily chronic purulent sputum pushes toward bronchiectasis.
2. Decide whether the airway can normalize.
Reversibility between episodes = asthma. Permanent dilation / no tapering = bronchiectasis.
3. Look for the “why.”
Atopy/eosinophils, aspirin/leukotrienes, PCD/dynein, CFTR/thick mucus, focal obstruction, post-infectious injury.

8 • Exam sheet

Integrated final-review sheet

Asthma & Bronchiectasis • Exam Sheet

Part I — Core framework & must-know content

Must knowBronchiectasis
Permanent dilation of bronchi/bronchioles from destruction of smooth muscle and elastic support. Infection and obstruction are a twinned process; either can precede the other.
Must knowAsthma
Intermittent, reversible airflow obstruction + chronic bronchial inflammation (typically eosinophilic) + smooth-muscle hypertrophy/hyperresponsiveness + increased mucus.

1. Bronchiectasis — solve it as a self-reinforcing structural disease

clearance problem / obstruction → infection → neutrophilic inflammation → wall injury → smooth-muscle + elastic-tissue destruction → permanent airway dilation → even worse mucus clearance
DomainExam-ready ruleWhat beats the distractor
SymptomsDaily chronic productive cough, foul-smelling sputum, dyspnea, hemoptysis; crackles/wheeze, cyanosis, clubbing possible.Asthma is more often episodic and dry; bronchiectasis is chronically purulent.
ComplicationsRecurrent bronchopneumonia; major hemoptysis; abscesses; cor pulmonale. Disease may be focal/diffuse and static/progressive.Hemoptysis = airway inflammation extending into adjacent artery.
ImagingAirway > adjacent vessel, non-tapering peripheral bronchi, tram tracks, signet-ring sign.The structural dilation is the diagnostic anchor.
PathologyMucus + inflammatory cells, epithelial injury, neutrophilic bronchiolitis, fibrosis/remodeling, squamous metaplasia.Practice question: increased squamous cells.
EtiologiesCF, immune deficiency, PCD, Mounier-Kuhn; TB/NTM, Staph, ABPA; tumor/foreign body; collagen vascular; COPD ± α1AT; ~50% idiopathic.You still search for an underlying cause even though ~half are idiopathic.
TreatmentTreat cause + airway clearance + prevention/vaccines + targeted antibiotics for exacerbations. Surgery only localized, non-progressive disease.Do not treat the CT finding alone; break the infection/clearance cycle.
NuancePCD: dynein/ciliary defect → poor mucus clearance → recurrent sinus/LRT infection → bronchiectasis. Dextrocardia/situs clue is high-value. Fertility problems may coexist.
NuanceCF: CFTR ion-transport failure → thick, poorly hydrated mucus → retained bacteria/inflammatory material → bronchiectasis. Same endpoint; different upstream defect.
TrapABPA: lecturer emphasizes it in the setting of asthma or CF. In difficult-to-control asthma, think high eosinophils/IgE and Aspergillus-directed testing.

2. Asthma — solve it as variable hyperresponsiveness + inflammation

trigger → hyperresponsive airway → bronchoconstriction + mucus + vasodilation/edema → reversible obstruction → late eosinophilic inflammation → repeated injury → remodeling
DomainExam-ready rule
Clinical patternParoxysmal wheeze, dyspnea, dry cough, chest tightness; often nocturnal/early morning; triggers include allergens, viral infection, cold, exercise, stress, smoke/irritants, aspirin/β-blockers.
Early phaseMinutes: mast-cell mediators → bronchoconstriction + mucus secretion + vasodilation/edema.
Late phaseHours: recruited inflammatory cells, especially eosinophils, sustain bronchoconstriction and injury.
RemodelingMucus-gland hypertrophy, smooth-muscle hyperplasia, sub-basement membrane fibrosis; repeated injury can make disease more persistent.
Path cluesCurschmann spirals = mucus casts; Charcot-Leyden crystals = eosinophil breakdown product and not asthma-specific; biopsy shows fibrosis + eosinophils + muscle hyperplasia.
Status asthmaticusSevere prolonged attack that can last days and can be fatal; requires aggressive treatment.

3. Atopic vs nonatopic vs aspirin-induced

AtopicNonatopicAspirin-induced
Core triggerEnvironmental allergenViral infection, pollutants, chemical irritants, drugsCOX-inhibiting drug
SensitizationIgE/type I; skin tests positive; family predisposition; rhinitis/eczema commonNo classic allergen sensitization; skin tests negative; family history less commonNot an IgE skin-test mechanism in the lecture framework
MechanismTH2/type-2 pathways; IL-4, IL-5; mast cells/eosinophilsViral/irritant pathways can enhance vagal bronchoconstriction and edemaCOX block → ↑ leukotrienes; LTB4 chemotaxis; LTC4/D4/E4 bronchospasm + permeability
ClueSeasonal symptoms + eczema/rhinitisAsthma pattern without allergy sensitizationAdult/new-onset asthma + sinus disease/nasal polyps + aspirin reaction
NuanceThe lecturer adds a newer type-2 vs non-type-2 molecular framework. IL-4/IL-5/IgE/TSLP biology matters because biologics can target these pathways. It overlaps—but does not perfectly equal—the older atopic/nonatopic labels.

4. Asthma testing — know what each test is proving

TestLecture findingInterpretation / trap
Spirometry↓ FEV1 and ↓ FEV1/FVC during obstruction; often normal between episodes.Variability is a defining clue.
Bronchodilator responseSlide: >12% and 200 mL increase in FEV1 or FVC.Course discrepancy: lecturer says this is the pre-2022 definition and notes current use of >10% with different math. Preserve both; recognize the slide criterion if it appears in course material.
DLCOUsually normal.A normal DLCO fits asthma; lecturer notes it can even be high but says that is beyond needed depth.
Lung volumesUsually normal between attacks; exacerbation can ↑ RV, FRC, TLC.That pattern = air trapping/hyperinflation.
MethacholineUsed when diagnosis unclear; FEV1 fall of 20% occurs at low exposure in hyperresponsive airways.Slide PC20 <20 mg/mL = older concentration metric. Lecturer says current course approach uses PD20 <400 µg.
Post-viral caveatHyperresponsiveness can persist 2–3 months.Wait 8–12 weeks after viral infection to reduce false positives.
Peak flow>20% AM–PM variability is suggestive.Tests variability, not just a single low value.
CXRUsually normal between attacks; hyperinflation and/or atelectasis during exacerbation.Use largely to exclude alternatives.

Part II — Testable distinctions, traps & question-stem decoding

6. “All that wheezes is NOT asthma”

ClueThinkWhy it beats asthma
Monophonic wheeze over glottisVocal cord dysfunctionUpper-airway localization rather than diffuse bronchial hyperresponsiveness.
Localized unilateral wheezeForeign body / tumorMechanical focal obstruction.
Wheeze + edema/heart failure contextCardiac wheeze / CHFDifferent upstream physiology.
Chronic cough after ACE inhibitorDrug coughNo need for variable obstruction.
Asthma + systemic vasculitic/neuropathic/cardiac cluesEGPAAsthma can precede multisystem vasculitis.
Poorly controlled asthma + high eosinophils/IgE + Aspergillus evidenceABPAAssociated fungal hypersensitivity process.
Episodic dyspnea with thromboembolic contextPECan mimic asthma symptom timing.

7. Treatment logic

Must knowICS is foundational. The lecturer specifically rejects bronchodilator-only thinking for asthma. All patients should receive some inhaled corticosteroid component.
TrapLABA alone = no. The lecturer warns LABA monotherapy increases risk of death in asthma; pair with ICS.
Step conceptLecture treatment ideaWhy
Lower burdenAs-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol / anti-inflammatory reliever (AIR)Treat both inflammation and bronchospasm even when symptoms are infrequent.
PersistentLow-dose maintenance ICS-formoterolDaily anti-inflammatory control + bronchodilation.
More persistentMedium-dose maintenance ICS-formoterolEscalate anti-inflammatory intensity.
SevereAdd LAMA vs higher ICS-LABA vs biologicAddress persistent symptoms/exacerbations and targeted inflammatory endotypes.
Why formoterol?It is long acting but has a rapid enough onset to serve in reliever-containing regimens, unlike other LABAs discussed by the lecturer.

8. EVALI — small section, very testable recognition

Stem
Vaping history + fever/malaise + dyspnea/cough/pleuritic pain ± GI symptoms + hypoxemia + bilateral ground-glass/patchy alveolar opacities + no infection.
Interpretation
Think chemical-pneumonitis-type EVALI. Vitamin E acetate was a leading 2019 consideration, but the lecture stresses multiple possible agents and variable pathology.
TrapDo not require lipoid pneumonia. Histology can show DAD/ARDS, organizing pneumonia, lipoid pneumonia, giant-cell interstitial pneumonia, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, DAH, acute eosinophilic pneumonia, respiratory bronchiolitis, or ILD.

9. Question-stem decoder

If the stem gives…First identify…Then check…Avoid…
Seasonal/nocturnal/exercise symptoms + dry coughVariable asthma patternReversibility, atopy, trigger historyCalling every wheeze asthma without localization/testing
Daily foul sputum + recurrent infectionBronchiectasis phenotypeCT dilation, no tapering, signet ringStopping at “chronic bronchitis” if structural clues are present
Childhood sinusitis + LRTIs + dextrocardiaPCDDynein/ciliary defectChoosing CFTR just because bronchiectasis is present
Aspirin + nasal polyps/sinus disease + bronchospasmDrug-induced asthmaLeukotriene pathwayPicking prostaglandin increase
Normal baseline spirometry but convincing asthma historyPossible intermittent asthmaMethacholine/variability testingExcluding asthma solely because the patient feels well today
Positive methacholine soon after URIPossible transient hyperresponsivenessTiming: 8–12 week wait; 2–3 month persistenceOvercalling a false positive
Localized wheezeMechanical obstructionForeign body/tumor contextAssuming diffuse asthma
Vaping + hypoxemia + GGO + negative infection workupEVALIExposure and syndrome patternDemanding one pathology subtype

10. Last-minute one-minute recall

Bronchiectasis
Permanent dilation; infection/obstruction cycle; chronic foul sputum; hemoptysis; signet ring / tram tracks; treat cause + clearance + targeted antibiotics.
Asthma
Intermittent reversible obstruction; eosinophilic; early mast-cell phase, late inflammatory phase, remodeling; normal DLCO; ICS foundation.
Three classic mechanisms
PCD = dynein/cilia; CF = CFTR/thick mucus; aspirin = COX block → leukotrienes.

Internal lecture discrepancy
Bronchodilator response: slide gives >12% and 200 mL in FEV1 or FVC; lecturer says this is the older pre-2022 definition and notes the current definition is >10% with different math. The guide preserves both rather than silently replacing the slide.
Internal lecture update
Methacholine: slide retains older PC20 <20 mg/mL language; lecturer says current practice/course framing uses provocative dose PD20 <400 µg. Both appear here with the older/newer distinction labeled.
Verification limitation: The guide is intentionally lecture-anchored. It does not independently verify 2026 external guideline wording beyond what the lecturer states and cites in the provided materials.
